newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour pledges tough anti-inflation stance.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour pledges tough anti-inflation stance.

text.p: Britain's Labour Party, expecting to return to power after 18 years in opposition, on Wednesday reinforced its claims to economic prudence by pledging to be at least as tough on inflation as the ruling Conservatives.

In a keynote speech, economics spokesman Gordon Brown said Labour would aim to limit price rises to no more than 2.5 percent a year and would reform the way interest rates are set to ensure the economy did not run out of control.
"We will be tough on inflation. Our aim is inflation of 2.5 percent or less," Brown said in a speech to an economic think-tank.

This target matches that set by current finance minister Kenneth Clarke, although Brown noted the government had not got inflation below 2.5 percent since December 1994 and had done so in only 11 of the past 52 months.
"We understand the need to tackle the causes of inflation at source... we will ensure decision-making on interest rates is more effective, open and accountable," Brown said.
"If we are to achieve our objectives for inflation, never again should interest rate decisions affecting the long term appear to be manipulated for short-term party political ends."
Labour is 20 points ahead of the Conservatives according to an NOP/Reuter opinion poll published earlier this week, with an election due within three months.

Brown, rejecting calls in the financial community for an independent Bank of England (BoE), said responsibility for interest rates would remain with the chancellor of the exchequer, or finance minister.
But he would come to his decisions after taking advice from a broad-based monetary policy committee in the central bank, and from a new Council of Economic Advisers within the Treasury.

Brown said that in order to avoid suspicions that the system was being manipulated for political reasons, a Labour government would publish a timetable for rate-setting meetings months in advance and announce decisions immediately they ended.

Aides said Brown had grown concerned that the monthly meetings between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and BoE governor Eddie George to set interest rates had become too personalised and at times too confrontational.

Clarke, who publishes the advice George gives him, accused Brown of planning to take decisions behind closed doors. But Brown's aides said the opposite was true, and the new system would be far more open and strengthen the BoE's advisory role.
Brown described the changes as some of the biggest since the 1940s and said they would help Britain to escape from the stop-go economic policies that had long bedevilled the country.

The new monetary policy committee -- agreed during private talks with the BoE -- would comprise the governor of the central bank, his deputy, two Bank of England executive directors and three or four outside figures.

The Council of Economic Advisers -- named after the group of economists that advises the U.S. president -- would replace the panel of independent forecasters, or "wise men", created to advise the chancellor in the wake of sterling's ejection from the European Exchange Rate mechanism in September 1992.
Brown's speech was intended to slot into place the last pieces of the macroeconomic jigsaw he has assembled recently.
He had already promised to adopt the Conservatives' spending plans for the next two years and to freeze income tax rates for the five-year life of the next parliament.
